paragraphs.text: This leaf comes from [Yiwu](greater-yiwu:where-it-is), in the north of Mengla County in Xishuangbanna, on the east side of the Lancang River. It is one of the old Six Famous Tea Mountains, and the town has long been where tea from the surrounding villages is gathered and processed. The name covers the town, the mountain and a wider area, so on a label it places the leaf in the region rather than in one village or plot; it is, in the trade's sense, [a market name](greater-yiwu:on-a-label).

The leaf was made into [ripe pu’er](shou:definition). It was wetted and heaped in a [damp pile](shou:wet-piling), where the microbes' own heat works on it. The pile is covered to hold that heat in, turned about once a week to let air through, and kept below about 65°C so the leaf does not char. After one to two months the leaf is dried. The method was developed to give in weeks what raw pu’er reached only after years of keeping, so this tea is ready to drink now rather than after a long wait.

brewing.text: Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
